source: Daw, Gershman, Seymour, Dayan, Dolan (2011) Model-based influences on humans' choices and striatal prediction errors
finding: First two-step task. Choices after reward depend on whether the transition was common or rare, so behaviour is not pure model-free. Closes gap 6 for Daw.
numbers: N=17 healthy adults (5 female, mean age 25.8), 201 trials in 3 blocks of 67. Hierarchical logistic regression: reward main effect p<1e-8; reward x transition interaction p<5e-5; transition main effect p=.5; stay bias p<5e-12. Median model-free weight 61% (model-based 39%), differs from 0 and 100% by sign tests, Ps<.005.
quote: the interaction between reward and the transition probability was also significant
limits: Small N. No exclusions were found in the page text (searched for 'exclu'). Later work shows instruction understanding shifts weights toward model-based.
agent_relevance: Confirms second-hand N=17. The 61% MF figure is the one that later work calls inflated by weak instructions; do not use it as a stable human trait.

source: Momennejad, Russek, Cheong, Botvinick, Daw, Gershman (2017) The successor representation in human reinforcement learning, Experiment 1 (bioRxiv full text)
finding: Passive learning task. Reward revaluation worked better than transition revaluation, as an SR learner predicts and as pure MF or pure MB do not. Closes gap 6 for Experiment 1.
numbers: 69 recruited; 4 dropped for not finishing in 1.5 h; 7 dropped for under 80% accuracy on an attention categorisation; N=58 analysed. Reward vs transition revaluation t(57)=2.89, p<.01. Reward vs control t(57)=10.14, p<.001. Transition vs control t(57)=9.05, p<.001. Control vs zero t(57)=1.2, p=.22. Final preference reaction times were slower after transition revaluation.
limits: Preference ratings, not actions. The mean revaluation scores (0.52 vs 0.45) were in figures, not in the text, so that pair stays unchecked. The 80% accuracy exclusion removes 11 of 69 (16%).
agent_relevance: Confirms N=58 and the direction. The asymmetry is modest (t of 2.89 in 58 people). Treat as a small, real effect.

source: Momennejad et al. (2017) Experiment 2 (sequential decision task, castle rooms)
finding: Replicates and extends with a decision task and a new policy revaluation condition. Policy revaluation has the same experience as reward revaluation but the same predicted pattern as transition revaluation, so it separates algorithm from difficulty.
numbers: 115 recruited on Mechanical Turk; all passed a 9-item instruction check at 100%; 27 excluded for not learning the policy in phase 1 in at least one condition; N=88 analysed. Four games per person, three-stage decision tree.
limits: Exclusion of 27 of 115 (23%) is large and based on learning, which may bias toward better learners. Exp 2 test statistics were not extracted this session.
agent_relevance: Confirms N=88. Policy revaluation is the human parallel of CogEval's policyReval, the task LLMs fail worst.

source: CogEval (Momennejad et al. 2023), contrast computed from Table 3 means and SDs
finding: The human asymmetry (reward easier than transition revaluation) does NOT show up as a consistent LLM pattern. For 3 of the first 4 models, transition revaluation scored equal or higher than reward revaluation. Partly closes gap 5.
numbers: Mean, SD for rewardReval vs transReval: GPT-4 0.67,0.40 vs 0.60,0.42; GPT-3.5 0.57,0.36 vs 0.59,0.40; davinci 0.34,0.25 vs 0.49,0.38; Claude-1 0.48,0.35 vs 0.55,0.36. Differences are 0.07, -0.02, -0.15, -0.07 against SDs near 0.4. policyReval for the same models is 0.21, 0.18, 0.13, 0.28. Temperature had no effect (chi2(11)=1.28, p=.53); 30 samples per prompt for the 3 OpenAI models, 1 for the others.
limits: No paired test run by the authors; per-cell n is not in the table, so only effect direction is given, no p value. Task is text-described graph navigation, not the human castle design. Models are 2023. Column order assumed from the earlier cross-check.
agent_relevance: The big LLM gap is reward change vs policy change (0.67 vs 0.21 for GPT-4), not reward vs transition. A scaffold should test policy revaluation separately.

source: Parks and Alharthi (2026) Predictive Maps of Multi-Agent Reasoning (arXiv 2605.11453), re-read for gap 2
finding: An SR matrix M=(I-P)^-1 of an LLM communication graph predicts robustness, but its spectral radius ranks cumulative error in the wrong order. Nearest measured case of a linear SR missing a failure mode, though it concerns the graph, not the policy.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 12-step state tracking, 100 trials per topology, 3 topologies. Condition number vs perturbation robustness rs=1.0; spectral gap vs consensus rs=0.5; spectral radius vs cumulative error rs=-1.0.
limits: Three ranks only, so rs of +-1 carries almost no weight (the authors say so). One 7B model. Not a test of SR memory when the policy changes.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: nobody changed an LLM agent's policy and re-measured an SR-style memory. This paper warns that a linear summary can hide drift.

source: Baumgartner, Spens, Burgess, Manescu (2025) Cognitive Maps in Language Models: A Mechanistic Analysis of Spatial Planning
finding: GPT-2 models trained on random-walk foraging build a map-like coordinate code; models trained for shortest paths stay path-dependent. Exploration data gives a map, goal data gives a heuristic.
numbers: Three training regimes in grid worlds: Foraging, SP-Hamiltonian, SP-Random Walk (hybrid). The Foraging model's reliance on past direction tokens vanishes by the middle layers (phase transition). The hybrid generalises better than its parent but keeps the path-dependent strategy.
limits: Small GPT-2 trained from scratch, not a prompted frontier model. No numbers beyond the abstract were extracted.
agent_relevance: Hint for building class-transition memory from all runs, not only goal-reaching successes.

source: Xiong et al. (2026) Unrewarded Exploration in LLMs Reveals Latent Learning from Psychology (arXiv 2601.22474)
finding: Tolman-style latent learning appears in RL post-training of LLMs: a stage without reward gives modest gains and a later rewarded stage ends higher than reward-only training. This is training, not scaffolding.
numbers: Math (six benchmarks incl. GSM8K, MATH500, AIME24, AMC23), GUI grounding (ScreenSpot variants) and GUI agent tasks; Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-VL-3B among the models. Exact deltas in Tables 2-6 not extracted. The paper says gains are larger on GUI agent tasks than on math.
limits: Training-time effect, one lab, gains described as modest. Does not test a frozen model with a graph in its prompt.
agent_relevance: Not a test of gap 4. Weak support for exploring before rewarding; do not use it for the scaffold.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) WebATLAS: An LLM Agent with Experience-Driven Memory and Action Simulation (arXiv 2510.22732)
finding: A training-free web agent with a persistent cognitive map from curiosity-driven exploration plus look-ahead simulation reaches 63.0% on WebArena-Lite. The structured map helps; the raw version hurts. Best direct LLM data for gaps 1 and 3.
numbers: WebArena-Lite success: AgentOccam base (Claude-4-Sonnet) 47.9; +CM-Raw 44.8; +CM 57.4; +hierarchical planning 50.9; full Base+CM+HL+LA 63.0; Plan-and-Act 53.9. On the Multisite split CM-Raw gets 19.2 vs 30.8 for base.
limits: Single benchmark, one base model, one run per cell (no CIs). Token cost per arm not in the text read, so not equal-token. The 'cognitive map' is a graph of pages and outcomes, not a discounted occupancy matrix, so it is SR-like only by analogy. Look-ahead was not isolated (only the full stack).
agent_relevance: Structured transition memory beat raw memory by 12.6 points (57.4 vs 44.8). Gap 1 is partly answered for structured vs raw, still not for SR specifically and not at equal tokens.

source: Ma et al. (2026) ProPlay: Procedural World Models for Self-Evolving LLM Agents (arXiv 2606.12780)
finding: A procedure graph of transitions among task stages, with a per-transition reliability record, used to preplay paths before each episode as soft guidance. It beats Reflexion, ExpeL, ReAct and world-model baselines on ScienceWorld.
numbers: ScienceWorld SR: ProPlay 37.4, ExpeL 36.3, Reflexion 32.2, ReAct 27.0, WALL-E 24.8, WorldCoder 24.8, LATS 18.9. Ablations: w/o graph 34.8, w/ retrieval 35.6, w/ random sample 35.9, w/ hard constraint 32.6. Hard constraint loses 4.8 points vs soft guidance.
limits: Gain over ExpeL is 1.1 points with no variance estimate. Table cells were read from garbled extracted text, so only ScienceWorld is quoted. Token budgets are not matched.
agent_relevance: The graph adds 2.6 points over no graph, and it must be soft advice, not binding. Support for a class-transition memory used as advice (gap 1, partial).

source: Hu, Van Durme, Andreas, Jhamtani (2025) ECHO: Sample-Efficient Online Learning in LM Agents via Hindsight Trajectory Rewriting (arXiv 2510.10304)
finding: Replaying failed attempts as synthetic successes for alternative goals helps an LLM agent adapt faster than Reflexion and AWM in XMiniGrid. Closest LLM analogue to replay between attempts (gap 9), but it relabels goals; it does not select by surprise.
numbers: Up to 80% better than vanilla language agents across XMiniGrid-Stateful and PeopleJoinQA; beats Reflexion and AWM in XMiniGrid (GPT-4o, temperature 0). Appendix: no offline method consistently beat the baseline on both accuracy and efficiency across 5 PeopleJoin organisations.
limits: Per-method numbers not extracted. 'Up to 80%' is a best case. The paper itself reports mixed results across organisations.
agent_relevance: Replay between attempts can work. No surprise-based selection here, so gap 9 stays open for the prioritisation part.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Possibility and Pass-rate Prioritized Experience Replay for LLM code agents (arXiv 2410.12236)
finding: Prioritised replay of failed programs, weighted by output probability and test pass rate, during fine-tuning. Prioritised replay in an LLM loop, but in weights, not in context.
numbers: Abstract claims better code-generation performance than baselines on several LLMs; table numbers not extracted.
limits: Fine-tuning, not a frozen-model scaffold. Priority is pass rate and likelihood, not prediction error. Only abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Shows prioritisation by a surprise-like signal is feasible; does not show an in-context replay buffer works. Gap 9 stays open.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think (arXiv 2505.13417)
finding: An RL-trained gate that picks Thinking or NoThinking per problem cuts length and raises accuracy on math. A learned cost gate with accuracy kept in the objective.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: response length down 50.9% (GSM8K), 63.5% (MATH500), 44.7% (AIME2024); accuracy up 4.1, 1.4, 1.6 points.
limits: Needs RL training and a 1.5B distilled model. The gate learns difficulty; payoff is not computed per problem. Not a plan-versus-act decision.
agent_relevance: A cost gate can cut tokens without losing accuracy (gap 8, partly closed for think/no-think, not for plan/no-plan).

source: Lee et al. (2026) DART: Draft-Agreement Routing for Training-Free Adaptive Thinking Budgets (arXiv 2606.23181)
finding: Training-free gate: sample two cheap no-think drafts; if they agree, answer directly; if not, set the thinking budget from draft entropy. Cuts thinking tokens and often raises accuracy.
numbers: Thinking-token use down 32-73%; accuracy up by as much as +9.0 points on Olympiad-level math and +22.5 points on code; signal tested from 0.6B to 32B and on API-only models including DeepSeek-V3.2. A supervised-router diagnostic found draft unanimity more informative than entropy or draft length.
limits: Numbers are best cases ('up to'); 'preserves or improves in most settings' means some settings lose. Abstract and method read; full tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Agreement of cheap drafts is a usable proxy for low expected gain from planning. Closest training-free test of a Kool-style gate (gap 8). It prices tokens, not payoffs.

source: Yu et al. (2025) Dyna-Think: Synergizing Reasoning, Acting, and World Model Simulation in AI Agents (arXiv 2506.00320)
finding: Putting world-model simulation inside the reasoning of a 32B agent reaches the best-of-n result of a 685B R1 with half the tokens, on OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena. Trained, not prompt-only.
numbers: Similar best-of-n to R1 at 2x fewer tokens on average; 32B Dyna-Think vs 685B R1.
limits: Needs imitation and Dyna training. Table row labels were garbled so only the headline claim is quoted. Compared on best-of-n, not single-run.
agent_relevance: One-step imagination can be token-efficient against long free reasoning, but this is trained. Gap 3 stays open for prompt-only frontier models at matched budget.

source: Wang, Ward, Zhang (2026) Rigidity in LLM Bandits with Implications for Human-AI Dyads (arXiv 2603.07717)
finding: LLMs in two-arm bandits behave rigidly. A hierarchical Rescorla-Wagner-softmax fit gives low learning rates and very high inverse temperatures. Qualitative patterns held across temperature and top-p settings.
numbers: Trials per condition as printed in the abstract: 200100 (likely 200-100, garbled); four decoding configurations. Symmetric rewards produced a stubborn one-arm policy driven by position; asymmetric rewards produced rigid exploitation below an oracle.
limits: Bandits, not a two-step design. No test-retest ICC is reported. Consistency across decoding settings is not reliability across sessions.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: some sign of stable LLM learning-parameter fits, but no ICC for an MF/MB index. Run repeated sessions before routing on a mode score.

source: Search log, 2026-10-31: gaps with no published test found
finding: Targeted arXiv queries for (a) CogEval-style revaluation on 2025-2026 reasoning models, (b) an LLM two-step task with the Daw regression on current models, (c) Kalman-TD successor representation tested on human data, (d) matched-budget imagination vs tree search, (e) SR-based LLM agent memory returned nothing that tests these. WebSearch hit its session cap after two calls (those also found nothing).
numbers: About 30 arXiv API queries and 2 WebSearch queries. Only the Kalman TD paper (arXiv 1910.02532, 2019) matched gap 7, and it is a machine-learning paper, not human data.
limits: Absence of hits is weak evidence: arXiv keyword search is crude, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited, web search was capped.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2, 4, 7, 10 are recorded as still open. Say 'this search did not find a test', not 'untested'.
